preamble: Depalatalization (hardening) of the palatalized voiced alveolar fricative [zʲ] to plain [z] before front vowels. In early Slavic, consonants were positionally palatalized before front vowels; after the fall of the yers this softness became phonemic. Ukrainian later hardened consonants before /e/ (зелений [zeˈɫɛnei̯] 'green', земля [zemˈlʲa] 'earth', where Russian keeps soft [zʲ]), and Czech underwent its 'main historical depalatalization' in the 13th–14th centuries, in which soft z’ merged with hard z (zelený [ˈzɛlɛniː], země [ˈzɛmɲɛ]).

examples.from: Old East Slavic зеленꙑи 'green' (cf. Russian зелёный [zʲɪˈlʲɵnɨj])
examples.note: Hardening of the fricative before original *e; the following [ɫ] is hardened as well.

examples.from: Old East Slavic землꙗ 'earth, land' (cf. Russian земля [zʲɪˈmlʲa])
examples.note: Same depalatalization before *e, whereas Russian keeps the soft [zʲ].
Old Czech soft z’ merged with hard z in the main historical depalatalization, completed in the 14th century.

examples.from: Old Czech země 'earth, land' (z’ before e)
examples.note: Depalatalization of consonants before e preceded the 14th-century merger of the remaining soft consonants.
